task_statement:
Research question (as posed on 2026-06-16, in the area of defensive suppression and counter strategy (best/avoid)):
Adhering to a suppression-conditional recommended mix predicts winning.

Data available on that date:
- NBA 2022-23 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2023-24 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2024-25 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2025-26 regular season (complete from 2026-04-13; partial before)
- NBA 2025-26 playoffs (complete from 2026-06-21; partial before)
- Sources: Per-game files from the NBA stats API: play-by-play (action type, sub-type, clock, period, score, player, shot distance and result), substitution rotation intervals, starters, defensive matchup minutes and partial possessions, box-score summary. Derived play-type possession records (initiator, play type, points) in a graph database built from the play-by-play.
- Units available to a study of this question (as recorded): 54 series

Your job is to decide, before any analysis is run, whether this question can be answered with this data, what has already been established about it, which methodological and statistical risks threaten a test of it, and either a pre-registration-quality design or a reasoned recommendation not to proceed.

methodological_questions: Does adherence to the recommended mix predict game or series wins beyond team quality?
Is the recommended mix derived independently of the outcome and of the evaluated games?
Is any apparent effect driven by CUT/PNR tagger floors or by selection/regression to the mean?

historical_evidence.finding: Closest prior test: series-level AVOID share vs winning. Game-level rho=-0.19 p=0.008 (inflated n, team-quality confound). Series-level rho=-0.26 p=0.07 (n=50), underpowered, with about 80 series stated as needed for p<0.05. Low AVOID-share bin 52.6% vs 25-50% bin 37.0%. Recorded verdict 'inconclusive'; failure mechanism A_unanswerable; still confounded by team quality (OKC disciplined and good). No validation recorded.

In holdout games, closer alignment to the recommended mix went with higher offensive efficiency: raw gap +5.18 ORtg, strength-controlled +3.27 ORtg (n=908 game-team rows). The outcome is efficiency, not winning. Regret is non-negative by construction. Validation was same-pipeline and no CI was stated.

BEST vs a constrained league mix: the headline gap (+0.269, n=283) is CUT-driven. Non-CUT gap is +0.010, p=0.1709, n=136, and L3 matchup non-CUT gap is +0.001, p=0.3277, n=47. Recorded as an adequately powered null for matchup-specificity. Limited by selection/regression to the mean.

Descriptive conformance of observed mix to the recommended opener in 4 playoff G1s (8 team-sides). Average |delta| was 4.5-24.0pp, and 4 of 8 sides best matched opener #3, not rank-1. CUT and PNR are muted by the tagger floor. There was no outcome comparison.

failed_approaches.what_failed: Series-level rank correlation of AVOID share with winning, with game-level pooling as support
failed_approaches.why: Series n=50 gave p=0.07 and was underpowered (about 80 needed). Game-level pooling inflated n. Both were confounded by team quality.

failed_approaches.what_failed: Claiming a matchup-specific recommended mix advantage
failed_approaches.why: The advantage was driven by CUT. The non-CUT gap was null, and selection/regression to the mean and small subsamples limited the result.

evidence_establishes: A directly related series-level test ([prior work][prior work], n=50) was inconclusive: the direction was negative for AVOID share but not significant, and team quality was not separated from the effect.
Alignment with the recommended mix was associated with higher efficiency (ORtg) in same-pipeline holdout games, including after strength control ([prior work][prior work]).
Apparent BEST-vs-baseline advantages were CUT-driven, and the non-CUT matchup-specific advantage was an adequately powered null ([prior work][prior work]).
Observed conformance to the recommended plan is often loose and affected by tagger floors ([prior work][prior work]).
evidence_does_not_establish: Whether adherence predicts winning, as opposed to efficiency, once team quality is controlled.
Whether the 'suppression-conditional' element adds anything beyond a generic mix.
Any out-of-sample, outcome-independent validation of the recommended mix.
Whether a series count of 54 can resolve the question; this is not established and looks marginal.
own_inferences: With 54 series and a plausible effect near rho=-0.26, a two-sided test has only about 45-50% power by a Fisher-z approximation, so a significant series-level result would be a coin flip even if the effect is real.
Good, disciplined teams probably adhere more and also win more, so a raw positive association is likely confounded by talent. The raw correlation could be an artifact.

The positive [prior work] efficiency result is weak support for winning. It uses the same pipeline that builds the recommendation, it concerns offensive efficiency rather than wins, and the non-CUT null in [prior work] suggests much of the gain comes from CUT.
Adherence is likely measured with floor-muted categories (CUT, PNR), so measurement error would attenuate any true effect.
The question is probably better posed at game level with series-clustered, team-quality-adjusted models, with the series-level test as a secondary check.
uncertainties: The exact definition of 'adherence' and of the recommended mix is not given. It may be the same as the AVOID share, or a distance to a model-recommended mix.
Whether the 54 series overlap with the 50 used in [prior work][prior work], and whether the recommended mix was fit on those games.
2025-26 playoffs are only complete from 2026-06-21, after the question date, so the series count may change.
The team-quality covariates available (pre-series net rating, seed, Elo) and their precision.
I did not read full family records beyond the retrieval summaries.

historical_effect.explanation: Without history, a direct series-level test on 54 units might have looked reasonable. [prior work][prior work] shows the same test was underpowered, inconclusive and talent-confounded at n=50, and [prior work][prior work] shows CUT-driven gains that disappear in non-CUT cases. This moved the decision from 'proceed' to 'proceed_with_changes': change the primary unit and outcome, require quality controls and a leakage-free mix, and not rely on a series-level p-value.

blocking_constraints.text: 54 series give about 45-50% power for rho about -0.26. [prior work][prior work] stated about 80 series were needed.
Adherence is entangled with team quality, since disciplined teams are also good teams. Without strong quality adjustment the association cannot be interpreted.
If the recommended mix is fit on the same games used to test winning, adherence is mechanically tied to outcomes. A strictly out-of-sample mix is required.

prior_work.summary: A closely related series-level test (AVOID share vs winning, n=50) was inconclusive and confounded. Mix alignment predicted efficiency but not winning, using the same pipeline for validation. A matchup-specific non-CUT advantage was rejected as an adequately powered null. Nobody has tested adherence to the suppression-conditional mix against winning with proper controls.

risks.text: 54 series is below the approximately 80 stated as needed. The game-level n is inflated by clustering within series.
Team quality, opponent quality, home court, and game state (score and garbage time) can drive both adherence and winning. Score-driven play-type shifts create reverse causation.
The recommended mix must be built only from data before the evaluated game or series, and not from the evaluated games.
If BEST/AVOID or 'suppression' labels are derived from points or results in the same games, adherence is partly outcome-defined.
CUT and PNR categories are muted by the tagger floor, which compresses adherence variance and biases the effect toward zero. The [prior work] headline was CUT-driven.
Teams or matchups chosen as suppressed or extreme will regress to the mean, which can mimic an adherence effect.
Adherence over about 100 possessions per game is noisy. Series-level averages are more reliable but there are few of them.
Many adherence definitions, mix versions, play-type subsets and bins invite a garden of forking paths.
Four seasons of league play-type tendencies are changing, and the playoff sample is partial for 2025-26.

design.estimand: The effect of a within-team one-standard-deviation increase in pre-registered adherence (negative L1 distance between observed and recommended suppression-conditional mix, with the recommendation fitted out-of-sample) on the log-odds of winning a game, conditional on pre-game team strength and opponent strength. Secondary: the series-level association between mean adherence differential and series win.
design.unit: Primary: team-game, clustered by series and team. Secondary: series (n=54), with adherence differential (higher-seed minus lower-seed, or team A minus team B) as predictor.
design.sample: All 2022-23 to 2025-26 regular season and playoff games available at a frozen data version. The recommended mix is fit with leave-one-season-out or strictly prior-games training. Games in blowouts (e.g. >20 points) or with garbage time are excluded or adherence is measured only in competitive possessions. Series are included only if complete.
design.power: At the series level, n=54 gives about 45-50% power for rho=-0.26 (Fisher z), so the series test is secondary and descriptive. The primary game-level mixed model must report the effective sample size after clustering, a minimum detectable odds ratio, and a bootstrap CI over series. Before unblinding, compute the minimum detectable effect from data variance. If the primary MDE is larger than the effect plausible from [prior work][prior work], label the result 'underpowered/inconclusive'.
design.controls: Pre-series team strength (prior net rating or Elo from games before the series), opponent strength, home court, rest, and starter availability. Adherence is also residualized against team season-average mix to separate a team's habitual style from game-specific adherence. Mix recommendations and adherence are computed only from non-CUT/non-PNR categories as the primary specification (tagger floor), with CUT/PNR-inclusive as sensitivity. Game state is controlled (score margin by period).
design.falsification: (1) Placebo: adherence to a shuffled or opponent-mismatched recommended mix should not predict winning. (2) Pre-trend: adherence in prior games should not predict outcomes before the matchup. (3) Negative control: the AVOID-share-vs-win association should vanish after team strength control, as [prior work][prior work] suggests; if it does not, it is evidence for adherence. (4) The CUT-excluded result must replicate the CUT-included one, given [prior work][prior work].
design.multiplicity: One primary hypothesis (game-level adherence coefficient, one adherence definition, one mix version, two-sided alpha 0.05). Secondary tests (series-level, subsets) are reported with Holm correction. Every variant tried is logged.
design.decision_rule: Supported only if the primary coefficient has the expected sign, its 95% series-clustered CI excludes zero after controls, the placebo shows no effect, and the sign persists in the non-CUT specification and across at least 3 of 4 seasons. Rejected if the CI excludes effects as large as the minimum effect of interest (pre-set before unblinding, e.g. OR 1.10 per SD). Otherwise inconclusive; a series-level p-value alone never counts as support.
design.data_version: Freeze a snapshot with a recorded date and hash. Use only completed series and games as of the freeze; if 2025-26 playoffs are partial (before 2026-06-21), either wait for completion or exclude them, and state the series count N before analysis. Record the code version of the mix recommender and play-type tagger.
